q1: SELECT C.DEPT_NAME, SUM(D.BUDGET) FROM COURSE AS C INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT AS D ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) INNER JOIN TEACHES AS T ON (C.COURSE_ID = T.COURSE_ID) GROUP BY C.DEPT_NAME HAVING SUM(D.BUDGET) > 100000 AND COUNT(D.BUDGET) > 10
q2: SELECT C.DEPT_NAME, SUM(D.BUDGET) FROM COURSE AS C INNER JOIN DEPARTMENT AS D ON (C.DEPT_NAME = D.DEPT_NAME) INNER JOIN TEACHES AS T ON (C.COURSE_ID = T.COURSE_ID) GROUP BY C.DEPT_NAME HAVING SUM(D.BUDGET) > 100000 AND COUNT(DISTINCT D.BUDGET) > 10

explanation: Q1 and Q2 are not semantically equivalent. The main difference lies in the HAVING clause: Q1 uses COUNT(D.BUDGET) while Q2 uses COUNT(DISTINCT D.BUDGET). This means Q1 counts all rows (including duplicates) for each department, while Q2 counts distinct budget values. This can lead to different results when there are duplicate budget values for a department.
counterexample_dsp: Create a scenario where a department has multiple courses with the same budget value. In this case, COUNT(D.BUDGET) would count all rows, while COUNT(DISTINCT D.BUDGET) would count only unique values, potentially causing the HAVING condition in Q2 to fail while Q1 passes.
